newsitem.title: USA: St Louis airport expansion may face trouble - report.
newsitem.headline: St Louis airport expansion may face trouble - report.

text.p: A proposed $1.88 billion expansion of the Lambert-St. Louis International Airport could face major revenue troubles with hub carrier Trans World Airlines Inc, according to a report commissioned by a city suburb that would lose 2,000 houses in the project.

Assuming cost estimates are accurate, revenue projections for the expansion plan rely on overly optimistic assumptions of federal funding and the continued viability of TWA, a Southern Illinois University assistant professor of political science said in the report for Bridgeton released Wednesday.
Airport Director Leonard Griggs Jr. declined to comment on the report, noting that the airport authority awaits a Federal Aviation Administration decision on the expansion.

TWA spokesman Donn Walker said the airline is confident in the airport authority's ability to complete the expansion and would not "get into a tit-for-tat with a political science professor from Illinois."
Walker added, "This is an issue for the whole metropolitan area and if the airport says it is able to do this, then we support them 100 percent."

Reached by telephone Thursday, Assistant Professor Scott Tarry said federal airport improvement program funds, projected as increasing in the plan, will decrease under President Clinton's recommendations.

Tarry also called TWA's viability as a generator of passenger facility charges at the airport critical and its continued role as a hub carrier key to the issuance of revenue bonds to finance the expansion.
"TWA can't compete with the low cost carriers like Southwest and it can't compete very well against the big carriers," Tarry said.
Tarry said he found it doubtful that an airline "barely surviving now with relatively low cost structures" could afford the higher landing fees necessary to finance the expansion.
Tarry also questioned the airport's contentions that it could find another anchor tenant if TWA fails.

"If TWA isn't there, they will need someone to generate the passengers, the enplanements and the revenues to pay for whatever has been accomplished with the expansion," Tarry said. "There is no likely candidate."

In an executive summary of the 24-page report, Tarry said TWA's financial condition would "undoubtedly" result in increased interest rates and more expensive insurance for a debt issuance that would "further increase the overall cost of an already expensive project."
Bridgeton funded the study with a $12,600 grant to Tarry and agreed that the results would be released whether pro- or anti-expansion, he said, describing himself as more often "pro-airline."
The expansion calls for demolishing 2,000 Bridgeton houses as part of a runway lengthening project.
An FAA environmental impact statement on the project is expected to be released in a matter of weeks.
